name: The Stefan–Boltzmann Law
statement: A body radiates energy in proportion to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.
statementAccent: the fourth power of its absolute temperature
meaning: Hotter objects radiate dramatically more energy, not just a little more. Because the total power emitted per unit area grows as temperature to the fourth power, doubling the absolute temperature multiplies the radiated power sixteenfold — a steep nonlinearity that makes temperature the dominant driver of radiative energy loss.
mechanism: Summing the black body's emission across every wavelength — integrating Planck's law over the whole spectrum — gives a total proportional to temperature to the fourth power, with the Stefan–Boltzmann constant as the accumulated factor. Real surfaces radiate a fraction of that, captured by their emissivity.

examples.text: A star's luminosity equals its surface area times the Stefan–Boltzmann emission, so measuring brightness and spectrum lets astronomers solve for a star's temperature or radius.

Because output scales with the fourth power, a modest rise in an incandescent filament's temperature sharply increases its radiated power and shifts its glow toward the visible — disproportionately brighter and whiter.
Balancing absorbed sunlight against fourth-power emission gives a planet's effective radiating temperature, the backbone of simple climate energy-balance models.

variants.name: Planck's law
variants.text: The parent spectral distribution; the Stefan–Boltzmann law is what you get by integrating it over all wavelengths to obtain the total radiated power.

variants.name: The grey-body form
variants.text: The correction for real surfaces: radiated power equals emissivity times the black-body value, with emissivity between zero and one accounting for imperfect emitters.

whyItMatters: It is the master law of thermal radiation, indispensable to astrophysics, climate science, and radiometry, and a rare case where an empirical discovery and an independent thermodynamic derivation converged before quantum theory explained both. Its fourth-power steepness is why temperature dominates radiative heat transfer.

working.text: expect radiated power to change far faster than temperature — a small temperature rise is a large jump in emission.
multiply the black-body value by the material's emissivity, and use the difference of fourth powers for net exchange between two bodies.
the law requires kelvin, so convert before computing radiated power.

limits: The law is exact only for an ideal black body, a perfect absorber and emitter. Real bodies have emissivity below one, sometimes varying with wavelength and direction, so the grey-body form is itself an approximation. It requires absolute temperature and describes thermal-equilibrium radiation; net radiative exchange between bodies needs the difference of their fourth-power emissions. Within these bounds it is a bedrock, exactly-grounded law, its constant now fixed by fundamental constants.
misreadings: It is not a linear rule — radiated power rises with the fourth power of temperature, so intuition that scales it directly with temperature badly underestimates the effect. And it describes an ideal black body; real objects emit less, in proportion to their emissivity.
origin: Established empirically by Josef Stefan in 1879 from radiation measurements, and derived thermodynamically by his former student Ludwig Boltzmann in 1884. It is later understood as the wavelength-integral of Planck's quantum law, with a constant fixed by fundamental constants.
